transcript.question: To start, could you walk me through your most recent ordinary working day, from the moment you arrived to the moment you left?
That's fine, let's make it smaller. What was the very first thing you did when you got to work this morning?
No problem. Think of the last drone you had your hands on: what were you doing with it?
transcript.answer: I was keeping the drone in working order by adding a new one to the fleet, retiring an old one, taking it out of service for repairs and putting it back, or sending it to charge. My company runs a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers, which differ in their carrying capacity, flight range on a full battery, sensors, and charging connectors.

transcript.question: Tell me about the last time you took one specific drone out of service for repair. What happened, step by step?
You mentioned that the models differ in capacity, range, sensors, and charging connectors. When do those differences matter in your own work?
transcript.answer: I need to know those differences because we run a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers, and their charging connectors are not interchangeable. That matters when I set up charging pads at our sites or when I send drones to charge.

transcript.question: Tell me more about setting up charging pads at your sites. What does that involve?
transcript.answer: I set up charging pads at our sites, and we have a few dozen of them. This is part of keeping our equipment in working order, alongside my work with the drones.

transcript.question: When you send a drone to charge, how do you decide which pad it goes to?
Let's move to something different. Think of the worst day you've had at work in the last few months. What happened?
Has anything ever gone wrong with a drone or a charging pad that you had to deal with? Tell me about one such case.
transcript.answer: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order by adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge. Regulators can ask my company to show how its drones have been looked after.

transcript.question: You said regulators can ask your company to show how its drones have been looked after. What exactly do they ask to see?
When you finish working on a drone, what do you record about it, and where?
When you add a new drone to the fleet, what do you have to do before it can fly its first job?
transcript.answer: I add new drones to the fleet as part of keeping the drones and charging equipment in working order. Beyond that, I don't know what I have to do before it can fly its first job.

transcript.question: Who tells you that a drone needs your attention, and how does that reach you?
When you put a drone back into service after a repair, who needs to know about it?
Is there anything in your work today that you double-check by hand because you don't trust what you've been told or shown?
If a new service were brought in for your work tomorrow, what would worry you most about it?
Imagine a drone has just failed in some way. What is the first thing you would want to find out?
What do you use today to keep track of a few hundred drones and a few dozen sites?
How do you decide that an old drone should be retired?
What do other people in your company need from you in order to do their own work?
Who outside your own company, if anyone, should be able to see information about your drones and charging pads?
transcript.answer: Regulators can ask my company to show how its drones have been looked after. I don't know who else outside my company should be able to see information about our drones and charging pads.

transcript.question: When you take a drone out of service for repair, what happens to the work that drone was supposed to do?
You said the charging connectors are not interchangeable. What happens when a drone arrives at a pad with the wrong connector?
Is there anything about your work that I haven't asked about and that you think I should know?
transcript.answer: I keep the drones and charging equipment in working order, which includes adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back, and send drones to charge. Regulators can ask my company to show how its drones have been looked after.

transcript.question: To start, could you walk me through an ordinary working day, from the moment you begin to the moment you finish?
That's fine, let's take it smaller. What was the very first thing you did when you started work today?
No problem. Think of the last job you dispatched, whenever that was. What happened with it?
Okay. Could you tell me, in your own words, what your job is?
transcript.answer: As a dispatcher, I plan and run the flights for my company, and I am the licensed person responsible for each one. I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I also have the ability to call off a flight.

transcript.question: Before you sign off a flight, what do you need to have looked at or satisfied yourself about?
You mentioned you can call off a flight. Can you tell me about a time you did that?
Let's try a different angle. What was the worst day you've had at work in the last few months?
All right. Who gives you the work you do, and who do you pass work on to?
I notice my questions aren't landing well. What about your work would you find easiest to tell me about?
transcript.answer: I can tell you that I work as a dispatcher for one of the drone operating companies, where I am the licensed person responsible for each flight. My job is to plan and run the flights, decide which drone flies and along which way, sign off a flight before it leaves, and I have the power to call off a flight.

transcript.question: Thank you, that helps. In doing that job, is there anything you check yourself, by hand, because you don't fully trust what you're shown or told?
If a new service were brought in for your work tomorrow, what would worry you most about it?
transcript.answer: I worry about things happening outside our control before and during a flight, like whether the load is ready, if the drone reaches its points, and when it arrives. It worries me that radio coverage is patchy, and reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. I also worry that the service runs on a single server, is updated and restarted during working hours while drones fly, occasionally crashes, and the companies accept a few minutes of interruption.

transcript.question: When a report from a drone arrives late, out of order, twice, or not at all, what does that mean for you at your desk?
You said the service can crash or restart while drones are flying. In the first minute after it comes back, what do you need to know?
More generally, then: when something has gone wrong with a flight, what do you need to find out straight away?
Going back to your worries about a new service: what else would you be afraid it might get wrong?
transcript.answer: I worry about instructions not getting through properly because the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are unreliable, meaning an instruction may get through twice and the sender often cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived. I am also concerned that batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and that a closure of airspace can come into force while drones are already in the air.

transcript.question: What worries you about an instruction reaching a drone or a charger twice?
Is there anything else you'd be afraid a new service would do wrong?
transcript.answer: I worry about several dispatchers planning at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. It also worries me that drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on, and that nobody watches every drone at every moment while one person may be responsible for hundreds.

transcript.question: Is there anything else you'd be afraid a new service would do wrong?
You are the licensed person responsible for each flight. What must never happen on a flight you have signed off?
How does your work connect with the fleet technicians and the airspace desk?
What can you tell me about what happens between the moment you sign off a flight and the moment it arrives?
What do you need most from a new service to do your job well?
What worries you about sharing a service with other drone companies?

transcript.answer: I worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, which causes reports from drones to arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. It also worries me that closures of airspace can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and that batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.

transcript.question: What in your work today do you not trust?
What would make a working day a really bad one for you?
What worries you about the people you depend on, or the people who depend on you?
Is there anything I haven't asked about that you think I should know?
When something goes wrong during a flight, what worries you most in the moments afterwards?
You said one person may be responsible for hundreds of drones while nobody watches each one. What worries you about that?
transcript.answer: I worry about nobody watching every drone at every moment, especially since one person may be responsible for hundreds.

transcript.question: To start, could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you begin until you finish?
transcript.answer: I keep the shared picture of the airspace by working with the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones grouping them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and sites have a limited number of places where drones can take off and land at the same time.

transcript.question: Think of the most recent closure you entered. What happened, step by step, from the moment you first heard about it?
No problem. When the authorities announce a closure, how does that announcement reach you?
That's fine. What is the first thing you do when you sit down to work in the morning?
Let's try a different angle. Thinking back over the last few months, which day at work was the worst, and what made it bad?
You said that when a closure is entered, you want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. What does "disruption" mean to you there?
All right. If a new service were built for your work, what would worry you most about it getting wrong?
transcript.answer: I worry about closures coming into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. I also worry because the service runs on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and it occasionally crashes.

transcript.question: Let's take the first worry. When a closure comes into force while drones are already in the air, what happens today?
And the second worry: when the server has restarted or crashed while drones were flying, what do you need to know once it is back?
Understood. Is there anything in your work today that you check by hand because you don't trust what you're shown?
Who do you hand work to, and who hands work to you?
Think of a moment when something has just gone wrong in the airspace picture. What do you need to know right away?
When you enter a closure, what exactly do you record about it?
transcript.answer: I record closures announced by the authorities, which can be planned ones with a start and end time, or sudden ones that apply at once. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves.

transcript.question: Tell me about one such amendment — say an area was widened. What did you have to do then?
What can a closure apply to — what is it that gets closed?
You mentioned zones that group corridors and sites. What do you use the zones for?
transcript.answer: I keep the shared picture of the airspace by working with the network of flight corridors between sites and the zones that group them. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce closures. I don't know anything else about what the zones are used for.

transcript.question: You also mentioned that sites have a limited number of places for take-off and landing. How does that come into your work?
transcript.answer: Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. I don't know how that comes into my work beyond what is stated.

transcript.question: Once you have entered a closure, who needs to know about it?
transcript.answer: I don't know who needs to know about it. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

transcript.question: How do you find out today how much disruption a closure caused?
You said the server is updated and restarted during working hours and sometimes crashes. Tell me more about what that is like for you.
transcript.answer: The service runs on a single server, and it is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying. It also occasionally crashes, but the companies accept a few minutes of interruption.

transcript.question: And what would the companies not accept in such an interruption?
You mentioned zones where flying is prohibited. How do those differ from closures in your work?
transcript.answer: The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, while they announce closures that can be planned with a start and end time or be sudden ones applying at once. Closures are also often amended during the day, for example when an area is widened or an end time moves.

transcript.question: When you look at the disruption a closure caused across customers, who else should be able to see that picture?
transcript.answer: I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

transcript.question: Can you give me an example of what would count as looking into one company's operations, something you should not be seeing?
transcript.answer: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations.

transcript.question: Is there anything about your work that I haven't asked about and that you think I should know?
transcript.answer: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, including the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

The service must never show that a point was reached, a load was ready or a drone arrived unless a report said so. For every flight in progress it must show when it last heard from the drone, so that "no report" is never mistaken for "all is well".

When a flight in progress has sent no report for longer than a set limit, the service must bring that flight to the attention of the dispatcher responsible for it. The interviews do not give the limit; it must be agreed.

When a drone restarts in flight and carries on, the service must go on treating its reports as belonging to the same flight. It must not treat the flight as ended or as a new flight, and must not lose what was already recorded for it.

The service must not assume a battery drains as planned. Where it receives a drone's battery level and that level is lower than planned for that stage of the flight, it must bring the flight to the attention of the responsible dispatcher.

Every instruction the service gives to a drone or to charging equipment must be made so that it can safely be sent again when the service cannot tell whether it arrived. An instruction that gets through twice must have the effect of getting through once.
The service must not treat an instruction as carried out merely because it was sent. Until something confirms it, the service must show the instruction as not confirmed.

The service must not depend on a person watching each drone. It must pick out the flights that need attention (affected by a closure, silent too long, battery below plan, instruction not confirmed, held from leaving) and present them to the responsible dispatcher set apart from the rest, so that one person responsible for hundreds of drones need not inspect each one.
The service must do all of the above while running on a single server. It must not rely on a second server being present.

After a planned restart, an update or a crash, the service must come back with everything it had accepted before still in place and unchanged: fleets, charging pads, care records, the airspace picture and closures, planned flights, sign-offs, call-offs, received reports and instructions awaiting confirmation.

It must be possible to update and restart the service during working hours while drones are in the air. After a restart or crash the service must be working again within a few minutes, and flights that were in progress must still be shown as in progress and followed from where they were.

On coming back after a restart or crash, the service must catch up on what fell due while it was stopped. A closure whose start time passed must be treated as in force and its affected flights brought to their dispatchers' attention, and silent flights must be detected. The service must not repeat any instruction in a way that makes it act twice.

The service must work at the scale described: several companies at once, a company having a few hundred drones of several models and a few dozen sites, several dispatchers planning at the same time, and one dispatcher responsible for hundreds of drones.
